page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question
Classification of Elements – Periodic Properties · 2 marks

steps.label: The definition
lines: Some elements of the second period show
similar properties to the elements of the
third period placed diagonally below them,
steps.why: Moving down a group makes an atom larger; moving one group to the right makes it smaller and more charged. The two moves nearly cancel, so the diagonal pair ends with a similar size-to-charge ratio and therefore similar properties.
common_mistakes: Writing that the similar element is directly below in the same group. It is one group to the right in the next period.
Naming the pair the wrong way, for example Li with Al. Each second-period element pairs with its own diagonal neighbour.
steps.memory_tip: One step down and one step right — the two changes in size nearly cancel, so the properties match.
steps.margin_note: The words second period, third period and diagonally must all appear.

steps.label: The example
steps.why: The relationship is a position on the periodic table, so the clearest example is the table itself: two rows of elements with an arrow joining each diagonal pair.
common_mistakes: Drawing the arrows straight down, which shows group-mates instead of diagonal pairs.
Leaving out the period names, so the two rows cannot be told apart.
steps.memory_tip: Two rows, three arrows, each arrow going one column to the right as it goes down.
steps.margin_note: The arrows carry this mark. Each one must start on a second-period element and end one group to the right below.

steps.label: The pairs
steps.why: Naming the three pairs in one line makes the example readable even without the diagram, and it is the line an examiner scans for.
common_mistakes: Writing C–Si as a diagonal pair. Carbon and silicon are in the same group, so they are group-mates, not diagonal neighbours.
steps.memory_tip: Three pairs only: lithium with magnesium, beryllium with aluminium, boron with silicon.
steps.margin_note: This summary line carries no separate mark, but it makes the example unmistakable.

insider_note: Examiners accept the answer without a diagram, but the two-row sketch with diagonal arrows is what makes the word diagonally impossible to miss.
